changes.before: Use meaningful sections for the title, navigation, main content, and footer.
changes.after: Give each part of an event page a clear job.

before: Semantic HTML uses element names to say what content is for. Semantic means “about meaning.” A header introduces a page or section. nav holds a group of navigation links. main identifies the central content of the page. footer holds closing or supporting information. These names help someone understand the page without relying on how it looks. A browser may not visibly style them differently. Their meaning remains useful to assistive tools and to people reading your code. Choose them for their job, then use CSS later to choose appearance.

This complete page gives an event clear regions. ```html Science afternoon

Science afternoon

Experiments

Sunday at the community center.

Experiments

Try making a paper helicopter.

Adults and children are welcome.

``` header contains the event title. nav gives a shortcut to a section. One main holds the event details, and footer finishes the page.

A landmark is a page region that assistive tools can help people find quickly. main and nav provide meaningful landmarks. For this ordinary page, use one visible main content region. Put the site's repeated navigation outside it so “go to main content” leads to the details, rather than repeated links. aria-label adds a short accessible name to a region or control. Here “Event sections” helps explain the navigation's purpose; it does not add a visible heading. Keep the visible link words clear as well. Native semantic elements usually provide the role without extra role attributes.

Headings describe an outline. h1 names this page's main subject. h2 names a section within that subject; h3 can name a subsection inside an h2 section. Choose levels for the relationship between ideas, rather than for the text size you want. In this event, an h1 followed by an h2 makes that relationship simple. A section groups related content and usually has a heading. A div is a general container with no special meaning; use it when you need grouping without claiming a more specific role.

This fragment belongs inside a main element. A link elsewhere on the page can use href="#tickets" to reach it. ```html

Tickets

Admission is free.

Group visits

Tell the organizer how many people are coming.

``` id="tickets" gives the outer section a unique identifier. The # in a link destination means an in-page fragment, a named place inside the current document. h3 is nested beneath the Tickets topic. Close the inner section before the outer section. Indentation makes the hierarchy visible, while tags define the real structure.

An anchor's href and a target's id must match exactly. href="#experiments" finds id="experiments"; a heading with the same visible word but no matching id is not that target. IDs should be unique within a document. Links need useful words, and the link should lead to relevant content. A correct landmark does not repair confusing writing or a broken target. Review the page's reading order from top to bottom, because that order is also important when someone listens to the page or moves through it with a keyboard.

For the exercise, put the event's h1 inside header, name nav with aria-label, put the Schedule link in it, and use one main for details. Put an h2 in the schedule section and give the section id="schedule" so href="#schedule" works. Finish with footer. The checks look for these regions and heading levels; they do not prove the whole outline or reading order is sensible. Ask yourself what someone would learn by reading only the headings, then follow the Schedule link and check that its destination exists.
after: Some HTML tags tell us what a part of the page is for. `<header>` introduces it. `<nav>` holds navigation links. `<main>` holds the main content. `<footer>` holds closing information. These names describe the parts; they do not choose their colors or sizes.

A landmark is a page area that tools such as screen readers can jump to. `<main>` and `<nav>` create landmarks. Use one visible main area here. `aria-label="Event sections"` gives the navigation a name for those tools; it does not show a heading on the page.

Headings show how ideas fit together. Use `<h1>` for the page’s main subject, `<h2>` for a section, and `<h3>` for a smaller part of that section. Choose the level by meaning, not by the text size you want.

A link to a place on this page starts its `href` with `#`. The name after `#` must match the destination’s `id`. Each id should appear only once on the page. The visible heading alone does not create a link target.

Wrap Art day in `<header>`. Put the Schedule link in `<nav aria-label="Event sections">`. Put the event details in one `<main>`, with a `<section id="schedule">` around the Schedule heading. Move `id="schedule"` from the heading onto that section. Add a `<footer>` with a short closing message.

before.question: You replace a generic div around the event details with main, without changing CSS. What has improved?
choices: The details now have a main-content landmark
The details automatically use larger text
The navigation links now lead to the details
before.explanation: main gives the region meaning for navigation and assistive tools. It does not set text size or create link targets.

after.question: You change a div around the event details to main. What improves?
choices: Tools can find the main content area.
Every link now points to the details.
after.explanation: `<main>` tells tools where the main content is. It does not change the text size or set up links.
